Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Those are the companions of Paradise, abiding eternally therein as a reward for what they used to do.﴾ The Mu'tazilah said: This verse indicates several matters:

First: His saying, ﴿Those are the companions of Paradise﴾. This conveys restriction (hasr, exclusivity), and this indicates that the companions of Paradise are only those who said, "Our Lord is Allah," and then remained steadfast. This indicates that the perpetrator of a major sin before repentance does not enter Paradise.

Second: His saying, ﴿as a reward for what they used to do﴾. This indicates the invalidity of the view of one who says that reward is bounty (fadl) and not recompense (jaza').

Third: His saying, ﴿for what they used to do﴾ indicates the affirmation of action for the servant.

Fourth: This indicates that an effect may occur in the state of the one who causes it, or that any effect may exist before that, as evidence that a prior action necessitated a later reward.

Fifth: The servant's being entitled to something from Allah, the greatest kind of this being kindness to parents. For this reason, He followed it with this meaning, so He said, exalted is He: ﴿And We have enjoined upon man goodness to his parents﴾. The discussion of a parallel to this verse has already been presented in surah al-'Ankabut and surah Luqman. In it there are issues:

The first issue: ʿĀṣim, Ḥamzah and al-Kisā'ī recited (bi-wālidayhi iḥsānan), while the rest recited (ḥusnan).

Know that iḥsān (kindness) is the opposite of evil conduct (isā'ah), and ḥusn (goodness) is the opposite of ugliness (qubḥ). Whoever recited (iḥsānan) has as his evidence His saying in surah Bani Isra'il: ﴿And to parents, kindness﴾ [al-Isra': 23], and the meaning is: We commanded him to convey to them kindness. The argument for the second recitation is His saying in al-'Ankabut: ﴿And We have enjoined upon man goodness to his parents﴾, and there is no disagreement about it. The intended meaning is also that We commanded him to convey to them a good action, except that He named that good action "goodness" by way of emphasis, as one says: "This man is knowledge and generosity." Ḥusnan is in the accusative as a verbal noun (maṣdar), because the meaning of "And We have enjoined upon man regarding his parents" is: We commanded him to be good to them (yuḥsin ilayhimā) with kindness (iḥsānan).

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿His mother carried him with hardship and gave birth to him with hardship﴾. Concerning this there are issues:

The first issue: Ibn ʿĀmir, ʿĀṣim, Ḥamzah and al-Kisā'ī recited (kurhan) with a ḍamma on the kāf, while the rest recited it with a fatḥa. It is said: both are dialectal variants, like al-ḍaʿf and al-ḍuʿf, and al-faqr and al-fuqr; and among non-verbal nouns: al-daff and al-duff, and al-shahd and al-shuhd. Al-Wahidi said: al-kurh is a verbal noun from "karihtu al-shay'a, akrahuhu" (I disliked the thing), and al-karh is the noun, as if it were "the thing disliked." He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Fighting has been prescribed for you, while it is hateful to you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 216], which is with a ḍamma. And He said: ﴿That you inherit women against their will﴾ [al-Nisa': 19], which is in the position of a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl). The second was not recited with other than a fatḥa. So whatever is a verbal noun or in the position of a circumstantial accusative, the fatḥa is better for it; and whatever is a noun, like "I went with it under compulsion (ʿalā kurh)," the ḍamma is better for it.

The second issue: The exegetes said: His mother carried him with difficulty and gave birth to him with difficulty. It does not mean the beginning of pregnancy, for that is not a difficulty. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿When he covered her, she carried a light burden﴾ [al-A'raf: 189], meaning the beginning of pregnancy, for that is not a difficulty. The fetus is a drop (nuṭfah), a clot (ʿalaqah), and a lump of flesh (muḍghah). When it becomes heavy, then ﴿His mother carried him with hardship and gave birth to him with hardship﴾ means the severity of labor pains.

The third issue: The verse indicates that the mother's right is greater, because He, exalted is He, first said: ﴿And We have enjoined upon man goodness to his parents﴾, mentioning both of them together, then He singled out the mother for mention, saying: ﴿His mother carried him with hardship and gave birth to him with hardship﴾. This indicates that her right is greater, and that the hardships reaching her because of the child are greater. The reports on this subject are well known.

[Page 14]

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And his carrying and his weaning are thirty months﴾. Concerning this there are issues:

The first issue: This is from the omission of a modifier (ḥadhf al-muḍāf), and the estimate is: "And the period of his carrying and his weaning is thirty months." Al-Fiṣāl means weaning (al-fiṭām), which is separating him from milk. If it is said: The intended meaning is to specify the period of nursing, not weaning, so how is it expressed with fiṣāl? We say: Since nursing is followed by weaning and is fitting for it, because it ends and is completed by it, it is called fiṣāl.

The second issue: The verse indicates that the minimum period of pregnancy is six months. Because the total period of pregnancy and nursing is thirty months, and He said: ﴿Mothers nurse their children for two complete years﴾ [al-Baqarah: 233], if you subtract the two complete years, which are twenty-four months, from the thirty, the minimum period of pregnancy remains six months. It is reported from ʿUmar that a woman was brought before him who had given birth after six months, so he ordered her to be stoned. ʿAli said: There is no stoning upon her, and he mentioned the chain that we have mentioned. And from ʿUthmān that he intended to do that, so Ibn ʿAbbās recited this to him.

Know that reason and experience also indicate that the matter is so. The practitioners of experiments said: The formation of the fetus has a determined duration; when that duration is doubled, the fetus moves; when twice that total is added to it, the fetus separates from the mother. Let us suppose that its creation is completed in thirty days. When that duration is doubled until it becomes sixty, the fetus moves. When twice that total is added to it, which is one hundred and twenty, until the total becomes one hundred and eighty, which is six months, then the fetus separates. Let us suppose that its creation is completed in thirty-five days, so it moves at seventy days. When twice that is added to it, which is one hundred and forty days, the total becomes one hundred and eighty and ten days, which is seven months, and the child separates. Let us suppose that its creation is completed in forty days, so it moves at eighty days, and it separates at two hundred and forty days, which is eight months. Let us suppose that the creation is completed in forty-five days, so it moves at ninety days, and it separates at two hundred and seventy days, which is nine months. This is the calculation that the practitioners of experiments mentioned.

Galen said: I was very keen to investigate the durations of pregnancy, and I saw a woman who gave birth at one hundred and eighty-four nights. Abu ʿAli ibn Sina claimed that he witnessed that. So the minimum period of pregnancy, according to the explicit text of the Qur'an and according to medical experiments, has become one and the same thing, which is six months. As for the maximum period of pregnancy, there is nothing in the Qur'an indicating it. Abu ʿAli ibn Sina said in the sixth chapter of the ninth treatise of ʿUnwān al-Shifā' (The Cure): It reached me from a source in whom I had complete trust that a woman gave birth after the fourth year of pregnancy to a child whose teeth had grown, and he lived.

It is related from Aristotle that he said: The times of birth and gestation of animals are fixed except for man; sometimes a pregnant woman gives birth at seven months, and sometimes in the eighth. A child born in the eighth rarely lives, except in certain lands such as Egypt; and the usual is birth after the ninth month. The practitioners of experiments said: What we have said, that when the duration of formation is doubled the fetus moves, and when twice that is added to the total the fetus separates, we have said only approximately, not as an exact limit. For it may increase or decrease by days, because no proof has been established for this precise calculation; it is only an approximation mentioned on the basis of experience. And God knows best.

Then he said: The period in which the fetus's creation is completed is divided into parts:

The first: When the womb contains the semen and does not expel it outward, the semen turns around itself, contained within itself, and becomes like a sphere. Since it is in the nature of semen to be corrupted by movements, it therefore thickens at this time. It is fitting that the creation of the semen is from a substance that dries out by heat, if the purpose of it is the formation of the living being and the firmness of its parts. The semen becomes foam on the sixth day.

The second: The appearance of the three blood spots in it:

[Page 15]

The first is in the middle, and that is the place which, when its creation is completed, becomes the heart. The second is above, and that is the brain. The third is on the right, and that is the liver. Then these spots spread apart, and red threads appear between them, and that occurs after another three days, so the total becomes nine days.

The third: The blood spreads throughout the whole, so it becomes a clot (ʿalaqah). That happens after another six days, so the total becomes fifteen days.

The fourth: It becomes flesh, and the three organs have become distinct, and the moisture of the spinal cord has extended. That is completed in twelve days, so the total becomes twenty-seven days.

The fifth: The head separates from the shoulders, and the limbs separate from the ribs and the belly; sensation is distinguished in some parts and hidden in others. That is completed in another nine days, so the total becomes thirty-six days.

The sixth: The separation of these organs from one another is completed, and it becomes such that that sensation clearly appears. That is completed in another four days, so the total becomes forty days, and it may be delayed until forty-five days. He said: The minimum is thirty days. Thus these medical experiments became consistent with what the Truthful, the one whose word is believed, reported in his saying ﷺ: "The creation of one of you is gathered together in his mother's womb for forty days." The practitioners of experiments said: When a miscarriage after forty days is cut open, its substance is taken out and placed in cold water, something small with distinct limbs appears.

[Page 16]

**Third issue:** This verse indicates both the minimum period of pregnancy and the maximum period of breastfeeding. As for its indicating the minimum period of pregnancy, we have already explained that. As for its indicating the maximum period of breastfeeding, it is due to His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And mothers suckle their children for two full years, for whoever wishes to complete the nursing﴾ [al-Baqarah: 233]. The jurists (fuqaha') have tied many rulings in jurisprudence (fiqh) to these two rules. Furthermore, once it is established that the minimum period of pregnancy is six months, then, supposing a woman gives birth to a child within these months, her reputation remains protected from the accusation of fornication and indecency. And supposing that the maximum period of breastfeeding is what we have mentioned, then if nursing takes place after this period, it does not produce the legal consequences of breastfeeding, and thus the woman remains covered from strangers. At this point it becomes clear that the purpose of establishing the minimum pregnancy as six months and the maximum breastfeeding as two full years is to strive to ward off harms, indecencies, and all kinds of accusation against the woman. Glory be to Him, beneath every word of this noble Book are wondrous secrets and subtle treasures, and minds fall short of encompassing its perfection.

Al-Wahidi narrated in *al-Basit* from ʿIkrimah that he said: "If she carries [the child] for nine months, she nurses him for twenty-one months; and if she carries him for six months, she nurses him for twenty-four months." But the correct view is what we have already presented.

* * *

Then He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿until, when he reaches his maturity (ashudd) and reaches forty years, he says, "My Lord, enable me to be grateful for Your blessing which You have bestowed upon me and upon my parents"﴾. Concerning this there are several issues:

**First issue:** The exegetes (mufassirun) differed in interpreting *ashudd* (full maturity). Ibn ʿAbbas, in the narration of ʿAta', said: "It means eighteen years." Most exegetes hold that it is thirty-three years. Al-Farra' argued against this view, saying: "Forty is closer in sequence to thirty-three than to eighteen. Do you not see that you say, 'I took most of the wealth or all of it,' which is better than saying, 'I took the least of the wealth or all of it'? A similar example is His saying: ﴿Your Lord knows that you stand [in prayer] less than two-thirds of the night, or half of it, or a third of it﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 20]. Some of these divisions are close to one another, so it is the same here." Al-Zajjaj said: "The better view is to interpret it as thirty-three years, because this is the time when the human body reaches completion." I say: The thorough treatment of this subject is to say that the stages of age in living beings are three. This is because the body of a living being is formed only by innate moisture (al-ruṭūba al-gharīziyya) and innate heat (al-ḥarāra al-gharīziyya). There is no doubt that innate moisture predominates at the beginning of life and is deficient at the end of life, and the transition from increase to decrease cannot be conceived unless there is a state of balance in the middle of these two periods. Therefore it is established that the span of life is divided into three parts:

The first: innate moisture exceeds innate heat, and in this state the organs are capable of expanding in themselves by increase in length, breadth, and depth. This is the age of growth and development.

The second stage, which is the intermediate stage: innate moisture is sufficient to preserve innate heat, without increase or decrease. This is the age of standing still (al-wuqūf), which is the age of youth.

The third stage, which is the final stage: innate moisture falls short of sufficing to preserve innate heat. This deficiency is of two kinds:
The first is the hidden deficiency, which is the age of middle age (al-kuhūla).
The second is the apparent deficiency, which is the age of old age (al-shaykhūba). This is a known classification.

Then there is another premise here: the cycle of the moon is completed in a period of twenty-eight days and some. When we divide this period into four parts, each part is seven days. For this reason they measured the month by the four weeks, and these weeks have great effects on the variation of conditions in this world. Having understood this, we say: The researchers among the experimenters divided the period of growth and development into four weeks (asābīʿ, sg. sābūʿ), and at the end of each of these four weeks the human being undergoes a kind of change that leads to his completion. As for the end of the first week of life, his organs harden to some degree, his actions also gain some strength, his weak and fragile teeth are replaced by strong teeth, and the power of appetite in this week is stronger in digestion than before. As for the end of the second week, heat strengthens, moistures decrease, channels widen, the power of digestion increases, the organs grow strong, and they harden with sufficient strength and firmness, and seminal matter is generated in him. At this point the Shariah judges him to have reached puberty according to the opinion of al-Shafiʿi (may Allah be pleased with him). This is the truth from which there is no turning away, because at this time, when innate heat has become strong, moistures decrease, and the brain becomes balanced, the psychic faculties—thought and memory—are perfected. Therefore he is necessarily judged to have attained full intellectual maturity, and for this reason the Shariah ruled for puberty and the imposition of legal obligations. How excellent is the statement of the one who fixed legal puberty at fifteen years.

Know that from the attainment of this state there follow certain conditions in the outward body:
One of them: the separation of the tip of the nose (arnaba), because the innate moisture there decreases, and so the separation appears.
The second: the protrusion of the larynx (ḥanjara) and the thickening of the voice, because the heat that rises at that time widens the larynx, so it protrudes and the voice thickens.
The third: the change in the smell of the armpit, which is the putrid residue that the heart pushes to that place. This is because when the heat of the heart becomes strong, it is necessarily strong enough to ripen the matter and push it to the soft glandular flesh in the armpit.
The fourth: the growth of hair and the occurrence of nocturnal emission (iḥtilām). All of this is because heat has become strong, so it is able to generate the vapors that produce hair and to generate seminal matter. At this time desire is stirred in girls, their breasts swell, and their menstruation begins, all of this because the innate heat within them has become strong at the end of this week. As for the third week, the person enters the limit of completion, and beard grows for males, and their beauty and perfection increase. As for the fourth week, these conditions remain in him complete and increasing; and at the end of the fourth week, the final limit is that the increase no longer appears. As for the period of youth, which is the period of standing still, it is one week, so the total is thirty-five years. Since this period may either increase or decrease according to temperaments, the limit in this matter was set as forty years. This is the age at which the perfection suited to the human being is attained, both according to the Shariah and according to medicine. For at this time the actions of the natural faculties become somewhat quiet, the actions of the animal faculty reach their ultimate end, and the actions of the psychic faculty begin with strength and perfection. Having understood this premise, it becomes clear to you that the human being's reaching the time of *ashudd* is one thing, and his reaching forty is another. For his reaching the time of *ashudd* is an expression of arriving at the end of the age of growth and development, while his reaching forty is an expression of arriving at the end of the period of youth. From that time the natural and animal faculties begin to diminish, while the intellectual and rational faculty begins to reach completion. This is one of the things that indicates that the soul (nafs) is other than the body, for the body at forty begins to decline, whereas the soul from the time of forty begins to be perfected. If the soul were identical with the body, then the same thing would have perfection and deficiency at the same time, and that is impossible. What we have stated and summarized here is set down in the explicit wording of the Qur'an, for we have shown that at forty the perfections produced by the natural and animal faculties come to an end, while the perfections produced by the rational and intellectual faculties begin to be perfected. The proof of this is His saying: ﴿until, when he reaches his maturity and reaches forty years, he says, "My Lord, enable me to be grateful for Your blessing which You have bestowed upon me and upon my parents"﴾. This indicates that the human being's turning toward the world of servitude and occupation with obedience to Allah arises only from this time. This is an explicit statement that the rational, intellectual, rational-speaking psychic faculty begins to be perfected only from this time. Glory be to Him who placed in this Noble Book these noble and sacred secrets.

The exegetes said: "No prophet was ever sent except after forty years." I say: This is problematic with respect to Jesus, peace be upon him, for Allah made him a prophet from the beginning of his life. Nevertheless, it must be said: the usual pattern is that revelation did not come to him except after forty, and it was likewise in the case of our Messenger (ﷺ). It is narrated that when ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAziz reached forty years, he used to say: "O Allah, enable me to be grateful for Your blessing," up to the end of the supplication. It is also narrated that "Gabriel came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: 'The two guardian angels are commanded: Be gentle with My servant from the youth of his age; then when he reaches forty, it is said: Preserve him and make him firm.'" The narrator of this hadith, whenever he mentioned it, would weep until his beard was wet. It was related by al-Qadi in *al-Tafsir*.

**Second issue:** Know that His saying: ﴿until, when he reaches his maturity and reaches forty years﴾ indicates that the human being is like one who needs his parents' care for him until about this period. This is because the intellect is, in a sense, deficient, so he must have his parents' care in securing benefits and warding off calamities. It also contains a reminder that the blessings of the parents upon the child, after his entry into existence, extend to this long period, and this indicates that the parents' blessings are such that it is almost beyond the human being's capacity to repay them, except through supplication and good remembrance.

**Third issue:** Al-Wahidi relates from Ibn ʿAbbas and a great number of both earlier and later exegetes that this verse was revealed concerning Abu Bakr al-Siddiq (may Allah be pleased with him). They said: "The proof of this is that Allah has specified the pregnancy and weaning here by an amount which is known to vary, sometimes less and sometimes more, due to differences among people in these conditions. Therefore it is necessary that the intended person be one individual, so that it may be said that this specification is a report about his condition. It is possible, then, that Abu Bakr's pregnancy and weaning were of this amount."

Then He, may He be exalted, said in describing that person: ﴿until, when he reaches his maturity and reaches forty years, he says, "My Lord, enable me to be grateful"﴾.

[Page 18]

Your blessing which You have bestowed upon me and upon my parents. It is known that not every person says this statement, so the intended person in this verse must be a specific individual who said it. Abu Bakr said this statement at around this age, because he was two years and some months younger than the Prophet (ﷺ). The Prophet (ﷺ) was sent at forty, and Abu Bakr was close to forty. He affirmed the Prophet (ﷺ) and believed in him. Thus it is established, by what we have mentioned, that these verses are suitable for Abu Bakr to be the one intended. Since this suitability is established, we say: we claim that he is the one intended by this verse. This is shown by the fact that at the end of this verse, He, the Exalted, says: ﴿Those are the ones from whom We accept the best of what they did and overlook their misdeeds; they are among the companions of Paradise.﴾ This indicates that the one intended by this verse is the most excellent of creation, because the one from whom Allah accepts his best deeds and overlooks all his misdeeds must be among the most excellent and foremost of creation. The ummah (community) has agreed that the most excellent of creation after the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) is either Abu Bakr or ʿAli. It is not permissible for the one intended by this verse to be ʿAli ibn Abi Talib (may Allah be pleased with him), because this verse fits only the one who uttered this statement upon reaching ashudd (full maturity) and near forty. ʿAli ibn Abi Talib was not in that condition, since he believed during his childhood or near childhood. Thus it is established that the one intended by this verse is Abu Bakr, and Allah knows best.

[p. 19]

**The fourth issue:** His saying, Most High, ﴿Awzi'nī﴾ (inspire me). Ibn 'Abbās said its meaning is "inspire me" (alhimnī). The author of *al-Ṣiḥāḥ* (the lexicon by al-Jawharī) said: "I awza'tuhu bi-l-shay'" means I urged him toward it (aghraytuhu bihi), so I awza' bihi, and he is muwza' bihi, meaning urged toward it. And "istawza'tu Allāha shukrahu" means I asked God to inspire me to give thanks, so He inspired me (fa-awza'anī), meaning I asked Him to inspire me and He inspired me.

**The fifth issue:** Know that God, Most High, relates that this supplicant asked God for three things. The first: that God enable him to give thanks for His blessings. The second: that He enable him to perform acts of obedience that are pleasing to God. The third: that He make his offspring righteous. Regarding the arrangement of these three things in the order mentioned, there are two reasons.

The first: We have explained that the levels of human felicity are three. The highest is the spiritual (nafsāniyya), the middle is the physical (badaniyya), and the lowest is the external (khārijiyya). Spiritual felicity is the heart's occupation with giving thanks for God's favours and blessings. Physical felicity is the body's occupation with obedience and service. External felicity is the happiness of one's family and children. Since the levels are confined to these three, God, Most High, arranged them in this order.

The second reason for observing this order is that God placed thanks before action, because thanks is an act of the heart, whereas action is an act of the limbs, and the act of the heart is nobler than the act of the limbs. Moreover, the purpose of outward acts is the states of the heart. God, Most High, said: ﴿And establish prayer for My remembrance﴾ (Ṭā-Hā 14), showing that prayer is required in order that it produce remembrance. Thus it is established that the acts of the heart are nobler than the acts of the limbs, and the nobler must be placed first in mention. Also, occupation with thanks is occupation with discharging the rights of past blessings, while occupation with outward obedience is occupation with seeking future blessings. Discharging past rights is like paying a debt, and seeking future benefits is seeking increase. It is known that paying a debt takes precedence over all other obligations, so for this reason He placed thanks before all other acts of obedience. Also, he placed the request for enablement to give thanks and the request for enablement to obey before the request that his offspring be made righteous. This is because the first two requests concern exalting God's command, while the third concerns compassion toward God's creatures. It is known that exalting God's command must take precedence over compassion toward God's creatures.

**The sixth issue:** Our companions said: The servant asked God, Most High, to inspire him to give thanks for God's blessings. This indicates that no act of obedience or deed is completed except by God's help. Had the servant been independent in his actions, this request would be pointless. Also, the exegetes said that what is meant by His saying ﴿Inspire me that I may give thanks for Your blessing which You have bestowed upon me﴾ is faith, or that faith is included in it. The proof is His saying: ﴿Guide us to the straight path, the path of those upon whom You have bestowed favour﴾ (al-Fātiḥa 6–7), meaning the path of those upon whom You bestowed the blessing of faith. Given this, we say: the servant gives thanks to God for the blessing of faith. If faith came from the servant and not from God, then that thanks would be thanks to God for His act, not for the act of another, and this is reprehensible, given His saying: ﴿And they love to be praised for what they did not do﴾ (Āl ʿImrān 188).

If it is objected: Suppose he gives thanks to God for what He bestowed upon him; how does he give thanks for the blessings He bestowed upon his parents? A man is obliged to thank his Lord only for what reaches him of blessings. We reply: every blessing that reached his parents from God, Most High, there reached from it some effect to him. Therefore God, Most High, enjoined him to thank his Lord for both.

As for the second request among the requests mentioned in this supplication, it is His saying: ﴿And that I do righteousness which You approve﴾.

Know that the thing which a person believes to be good has two types:

One: that which is good in his own view and is also good in the sight of God, Most High.

Two: that which he thinks is good but is not good in the sight of God, Most High. Since he divided what he considers good into these two types, he asked God to enable him to perform a righteous deed that is good in God's sight and pleasing to God.

The third request mentioned in this verse is His saying: ﴿And make righteous for me my offspring﴾, because that is among the greatest of God's blessings upon a parent, as Ibrāhīm, peace be upon him, said: ﴿And keep me and my sons away from worshipping idols﴾ (Ibrāhīm 35). If it is asked: what is the meaning of "fī" (in) in His saying ﴿And make righteous for me in my offspring﴾? We reply: the sense of the sentence is: grant me righteousness in my offspring and place it in them.

* * *

Know that when God, Most High, related of this supplicant that he asked for these three things, He then said: ﴿Indeed I have repented to You, and indeed I am of the Muslims﴾. The meaning is that supplication is not valid except with repentance, and except with being among the Muslims. Thus it is made clear that I only proceeded to this supplication after I had repented to You from disbelief and from every abomination, and after I had entered Islam and submission to the command of God and His decree.

Know that those who said this verse was revealed concerning Abū Bakr said: Abū Bakr's parents both embraced Islam, and this did not happen to anyone among the Companions and the Emigrants, that both of his parents embraced Islam, except him. His father was Abū Quḥāfa 'Uthmān ibn 'Amr, and his mother was Umm al-Khayr bint Ṣakhr ibn 'Amr. As for His saying ﴿And that I do righteousness which You approve﴾, Ibn 'Abbās said: God granted his request, so he freed nine believers who were being tortured for God, among them Bilāl and 'Āmir ibn Fuhayra. He did not leave any good deed undone without God helping him to it. As for His saying, Most High, ﴿And make righteous for me my offspring﴾, Ibn 'Abbās said: none of Abū Bakr's children, male or female, remained who had not believed. And it did not happen to any of the Companions that both his parents and all his children, male and female, embraced Islam, except Abū Bakr.

* * *

Then God, Most High, said: ﴿Those are they from whom We accept the best of what they did﴾. That is, the people of this statement. ﴿Those from whom We accept﴾ was read with a dammah on the yā' (nataqabbalu, in the passive form), and it was read with an open nūn (nataqabbalu, in the active first-person plural). Likewise (natajāwazu). Both have the same meaning, because although the verb is in the passive form, it is known that it refers to God, glorified and exalted be He. It is like His saying: ﴿Their past will be forgiven for them﴾ (al-Anfāl 38). By His saying ﴿Those are they from whom We accept the best of what they did﴾ [p. 20], He clarified that whoever has been mentioned earlier among those who make this supplication and follow this path that has been mentioned, ﴿from them We accept﴾. Acceptance from God is His making reward obligatory for them for their deed. If it is asked: Why did God, Most High, say ﴿the best of what they did﴾, when God accepts the best and what is less than it? We reply: the answer has several aspects.

The first: what is meant by "the best" is "the good," as in His saying: ﴿And follow the best of what has been sent down to you from your Lord﴾ (al-Zumar 55). It is like their saying: "al-Nāqiṣ and al-Ashajj are the two most just of the Banū Marwān," meaning the two just ones of the Banū Marwān.

The second: the good of deeds is the permissible (mubāḥ) that carries neither reward nor punishment, while the best is what differs from that, namely everything that is recommended (mandūb) or obligatory (wājib).

* * *

Then God, Most High, said: ﴿And We overlook their evil deeds﴾. The meaning is that God, Most High, accepts their acts of obedience and overlooks their evil deeds. Then He said: ﴿among the companions of Paradise﴾. The author of *al-Kashshāf* (al-Zamakhsharī) said: the meaning of this statement is like your saying: "The prince honoured me among two hundred of his companions," meaning he honoured me among the group of those he honoured, and counted me among them. Its position is accusative as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), in the sense of "being and counted among the companions of Paradise." His saying ﴿a true promise﴾ is an emphatic infinitive (maṣdar mu'akkid), because His saying "We accept, We overlook" is a promise from God to them of acceptance and overlooking. The purpose is to show that God, Most High, treats one whose attribute is what we have mentioned with this reward, and this is a promise from God, Most High; so He made clear that it is true, and there is no doubt in it.

[p. 19]

**The fourth issue:** His saying, Most High, ﴿Awzi'nī﴾ (inspire me). Ibn 'Abbās said its meaning is "inspire me" (alhimnī). The author of *al-Ṣiḥāḥ* (the lexicon by al-Jawharī) said: "I awza'tuhu bi-l-shay'" means I urged him toward it (aghraytuhu bihi), so I awza' bihi, and he is muwza' bihi, meaning urged toward it. And "istawza'tu Allāha shukrahu" means I asked God to inspire me to give thanks, so He inspired me (fa-awza'anī), meaning I asked Him to inspire me and He inspired me.

**The fifth issue:** Know that God, Most High, relates that this supplicant asked God for three things. The first: that God enable him to give thanks for His blessings. The second: that He enable him to perform acts of obedience that are pleasing to God. The third: that He make his offspring righteous. Regarding the arrangement of these three things in the order mentioned, there are two reasons.

The first: We have explained that the levels of human felicity are three. The highest is the spiritual (nafsāniyya), the middle is the physical (badaniyya), and the lowest is the external (khārijiyya). Spiritual felicity is the heart's occupation with giving thanks for God's favours and blessings. Physical felicity is the body's occupation with obedience and service. External felicity is the happiness of one's family and children. Since the levels are confined to these three, God, Most High, arranged them in this order.

The second reason for observing this order is that God placed thanks before action, because thanks is an act of the heart, whereas action is an act of the limbs, and the act of the heart is nobler than the act of the limbs. Moreover, the purpose of outward acts is the states of the heart. God, Most High, said: ﴿And establish prayer for My remembrance﴾ (Ṭā-Hā 14), showing that prayer is required in order that it produce remembrance. Thus it is established that the acts of the heart are nobler than the acts of the limbs, and the nobler must be placed first in mention. Also, occupation with thanks is occupation with discharging the rights of past blessings, while occupation with outward obedience is occupation with seeking future blessings. Discharging past rights is like paying a debt, and seeking future benefits is seeking increase. It is known that paying a debt takes precedence over all other obligations, so for this reason He placed thanks before all other acts of obedience. Also, he placed the request for enablement to give thanks and the request for enablement to obey before the request that his offspring be made righteous. This is because the first two requests concern exalting God's command, while the third concerns compassion toward God's creatures. It is known that exalting God's command must take precedence over compassion toward God's creatures.

**The sixth issue:** Our companions said: The servant asked God, Most High, to inspire him to give thanks for God's blessings. This indicates that no act of obedience or deed is completed except by God's help. Had the servant been independent in his actions, this request would be pointless. Also, the exegetes said that what is meant by His saying ﴿Inspire me that I may give thanks for Your blessing which You have bestowed upon me﴾ is faith, or that faith is included in it. The proof is His saying: ﴿Guide us to the straight path, the path of those upon whom You have bestowed favour﴾ (al-Fātiḥa 6–7), meaning the path of those upon whom You bestowed the blessing of faith. Given this, we say: the servant gives thanks to God for the blessing of faith. If faith came from the servant and not from God, then that thanks would be thanks to God for His act, not for the act of another, and this is reprehensible, given His saying: ﴿And they love to be praised for what they did not do﴾ (Āl ʿImrān 188).

If it is objected: Suppose he gives thanks to God for what He bestowed upon him; how does he give thanks for the blessings He bestowed upon his parents? A man is obliged to thank his Lord only for what reaches him of blessings. We reply: every blessing that reached his parents from God, Most High, there reached from it some effect to him. Therefore God, Most High, enjoined him to thank his Lord for both.

As for the second request among the requests mentioned in this supplication, it is His saying: ﴿And that I do righteousness which You approve﴾.

Know that the thing which a person believes to be good has two types:

One: that which is good in his own view and is also good in the sight of God, Most High.

Two: that which he thinks is good but is not good in the sight of God, Most High. Since he divided what he considers good into these two types, he asked God to enable him to perform a righteous deed that is good in God's sight and pleasing to God.

The third request mentioned in this verse is His saying: ﴿And make righteous for me my offspring﴾, because that is among the greatest of God's blessings upon a parent, as Ibrāhīm, peace be upon him, said: ﴿And keep me and my sons away from worshipping idols﴾ (Ibrāhīm 35). If it is asked: what is the meaning of "fī" (in) in His saying ﴿And make righteous for me in my offspring﴾? We reply: the sense of the sentence is: grant me righteousness in my offspring and place it in them.

* * *

Know that when God, Most High, related of this supplicant that he asked for these three things, He then said: ﴿Indeed I have repented to You, and indeed I am of the Muslims﴾. The meaning is that supplication is not valid except with repentance, and except with being among the Muslims. Thus it is made clear that I only proceeded to this supplication after I had repented to You from disbelief and from every abomination, and after I had entered Islam and submission to the command of God and His decree.

Know that those who said this verse was revealed concerning Abū Bakr said: Abū Bakr's parents both embraced Islam, and this did not happen to anyone among the Companions and the Emigrants, that both of his parents embraced Islam, except him. His father was Abū Quḥāfa 'Uthmān ibn 'Amr, and his mother was Umm al-Khayr bint Ṣakhr ibn 'Amr. As for His saying ﴿And that I do righteousness which You approve﴾, Ibn 'Abbās said: God granted his request, so he freed nine believers who were being tortured for God, among them Bilāl and 'Āmir ibn Fuhayra. He did not leave any good deed undone without God helping him to it. As for His saying, Most High, ﴿And make righteous for me my offspring﴾, Ibn 'Abbās said: none of Abū Bakr's children, male or female, remained who had not believed. And it did not happen to any of the Companions that both his parents and all his children, male and female, embraced Islam, except Abū Bakr.

* * *

Then God, Most High, said: ﴿Those are they from whom We accept the best of what they did﴾. That is, the people of this statement. ﴿Those from whom We accept﴾ was read with a dammah on the yā' (nataqabbalu, in the passive form), and it was read with an open nūn (nataqabbalu, in the active first-person plural). Likewise (natajāwazu). Both have the same meaning, because although the verb is in the passive form, it is known that it refers to God, glorified and exalted be He. It is like His saying: ﴿Their past will be forgiven for them﴾ (al-Anfāl 38). By His saying ﴿Those are they from whom We accept the best of what they did﴾ [p. 20], He clarified that whoever has been mentioned earlier among those who make this supplication and follow this path that has been mentioned, ﴿from them We accept﴾. Acceptance from God is His making reward obligatory for them for their deed. If it is asked: Why did God, Most High, say ﴿the best of what they did﴾, when God accepts the best and what is less than it? We reply: the answer has several aspects.

The first: what is meant by "the best" is "the good," as in His saying: ﴿And follow the best of what has been sent down to you from your Lord﴾ (al-Zumar 55). It is like their saying: "al-Nāqiṣ and al-Ashajj are the two most just of the Banū Marwān," meaning the two just ones of the Banū Marwān.

The second: the good of deeds is the permissible (mubāḥ) that carries neither reward nor punishment, while the best is what differs from that, namely everything that is recommended (mandūb) or obligatory (wājib).

* * *

Then God, Most High, said: ﴿And We overlook their evil deeds﴾. The meaning is that God, Most High, accepts their acts of obedience and overlooks their evil deeds. Then He said: ﴿among the companions of Paradise﴾. The author of *al-Kashshāf* (al-Zamakhsharī) said: the meaning of this statement is like your saying: "The prince honoured me among two hundred of his companions," meaning he honoured me among the group of those he honoured, and counted me among them. Its position is accusative as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), in the sense of "being and counted among the companions of Paradise." His saying ﴿a true promise﴾ is an emphatic infinitive (maṣdar mu'akkid), because His saying "We accept, We overlook" is a promise from God to them of acceptance and overlooking. The purpose is to show that God, Most High, treats one whose attribute is what we have mentioned with this reward, and this is a promise from God, Most High; so He made clear that it is true, and there is no doubt in it.

The Exalted said: ﴿And he who says to his parents, "Uff to you both! Do you threaten me that I will be brought forth, when generations have passed before me?" While they both call upon God for help, [saying], "Woe to you! Believe, for the promise of God is true." But he says, "This is nothing but the myths of the former peoples."﴾ ﴿Those are the ones upon whom the Word has been justified, among nations that passed away before them of jinn and mankind. Indeed, they were losers.﴾ ﴿And for each are degrees of what they have done, that He may fully compensate them for their deeds, and they will not be wronged.﴾ ﴿And on the Day those who disbelieved are exposed to the Fire: "You squandered your good things in your worldly life and enjoyed them. So today you will be recompensed with the punishment of humiliation, for what you were arrogant about in the earth without right and for what you used to defy."﴾

Know that when the Exalted described the dutiful son toward his parents in the previous verse, He described the disobedient son toward his parents in this verse, saying: ﴿And he who says to his parents, "Uff to you both!"﴾ Concerning this verse there are two opinions:

The first: it was revealed concerning ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Abī Bakr. They said: his parents used to call him to Islam and he refused, saying: "Uff to you both!" Those who held this view argued for its soundness: when Muʿāwiyah wrote to Marwān to take the allegiance of the people for Yazīd, ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Abī Bakr said: "You have brought this as a Heraclian (imperial) matter! Do you pledge allegiance for your sons?" Then Marwān said: "O people, this is the one of whom God said: ﴿And he who says to his parents, 'Uff to you both!'﴾"

The second opinion: the verse does not mean a specific person, but rather everyone who has this attribute, namely everyone whose parents called him to the true religion and he rejected and denied it. This second opinion is the correct one according to us, and several points indicate it:

The first: God described this one who said to his parents, "Uff to you both! Do you threaten me," with His words: ﴿Those are the ones upon whom the Word has been justified, among nations that passed away before them of jinn and mankind, indeed they were losers.﴾ There is no doubt that ʿAbd al-Raḥmān believed and his Islam was good, and he was among the leaders of the Muslims; so applying the verse to him is invalid. If they say: it is reported that when his parents called him to Islam and informed him of resurrection after death, he said: "Do you threaten me that I will be brought forth" from the grave, meaning: that I will be raised after death; ﴿when generations have passed before me﴾, meaning the earlier nations, and I have not seen anyone of them raised; so where is ʿAbd Allāh ibn Judʿān, and where is so-and-so? Knowing this, we say: His words ﴿Those are the ones upon whom the Word has been justified﴾ refer to those polytheists whom ʿAbd al-Raḥmān mentioned, who died before him, and they are the ones upon whom the Word has been justified. In sum, it returns to those pointed to by His words ﴿when generations have passed before me﴾, not to the one referred to by His words ﴿And he who says to his parents, "Uff to you both!"﴾. This is what al-Kalbī stated in answering that objection, and it is sound.

The second point, in refuting that view: it is reported that when Marwān addressed ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Abī Bakr with those words, ʿĀʾishah heard it and became angry and said: "By God, it is not about him, but God cursed your father while you were in his loins."

The third point, and it is the strongest: it is said that God described the dutiful son toward his parents in the previous verse and described the disobedient son toward his parents in this verse, and He mentioned among the attributes of that son that he went so far in disobedience that when his parents called him to the true religion, which is affirmation of resurrection and the Day of Judgment, he persisted in denial, refused, and was arrogant, and he relied in that denial on base doubts and feeble words. Since this is so, the intended meaning is every son who has the attributes mentioned, and there is absolutely no need to restrict the general expression to a specific individual.

The author of al-Kashshāf said: "Uff" has been read with fatḥah and kasrah without tanwīn, and with the three vowels with tanwīn. It is a sound which, when a person utters it, is recognized as an expression of irritation, just as when one says "ḥass," it is recognized as an expression of pain. The lām is for specification: its meaning is that this "uff" is specifically for you both, and on your account, not for others. "Ataʿidānanī" has been read with two nūns, with one of them, and "ataʿiddānī" with assimilation. Some read "ataʿidānanī" with a fatḥah on the nūn, as though they found the combination of two nūns, two kasrahs and a yāʾ heavy, so they opened the first for lightening, just as those who assimilated did, and those who dropped one of them.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿that I will be brought forth﴾, i.e., that I will be raised and brought out from the earth. It has been read "akhruja", and "when generations have passed before me", meaning that none of them has been raised.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿While they both call upon God for help﴾, i.e., the two parents call upon God for help. If they say: should it not have been said "yastaghīthāni bi-llāh" (call upon God for help)? We reply: the answer is in two respects:

The first: the meaning is that they both seek God's help against his disbelief and denial, so when the preposition was omitted, the verb was connected directly.

The second: it is permissible to say the bāʾ was omitted, because by "istighāthah" is meant here supplication, as the exegetes said: "they both call upon God." Since supplication is intended by istighāthah, the preposition was omitted, because supplication does not require it. His words ﴿Woe to you!﴾ mean: they say to him, "Woe to you!" ﴿Believe﴾, i.e., affirm resurrection. This is a supplication against him for perdition, but what is intended by it is urging and encouraging him toward faith, not the literal reality of destruction.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿for the promise of God﴾ regarding resurrection is true, so he says to them: "What is this that you say about the matter of resurrection, and call me to it?" ﴿This is nothing but the myths of the former peoples.﴾

* * *

Then God said: ﴿Those are the ones upon whom the Word has been justified﴾, i.e., the word of punishment has been justified against them. Here there are two opinions:

Those who say the verse was revealed concerning ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Abī Bakr say that those upon whom the word of punishment has been justified are the generations who passed away before him. Those who say it does not refer to ʿAbd al-Raḥmān, but to every son who has the stated attribute, say that this threat is specific to them. His words ﴿among nations﴾ are parallel to His words ﴿among the companions of the Garden﴾, and we have mentioned that it is parallel to the saying: "The Amir honored me among people of his companions," meaning he honored me among those whom he honored from among them.

* * *

Then God said: ﴿Indeed, they were losers.﴾ It has been read "anna" with a fatḥah, meaning he believed that the promise of God is true.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿And for each are degrees of what they have done﴾, and concerning this there are two opinions:

The first: God mentioned the dutiful son, then followed him with mention of the disobedient son, so His words ﴿And for each are degrees of what they have done﴾ are specific to the believers, because the believing son who is dutiful to his parents has varying degrees and different ranks in this matter.

The second opinion: His words ﴿And for each are degrees of what they have done﴾ refer to both groups, meaning that each of the two groups has degrees in faith, disbelief, obedience and disobedience. If they say: how is it permissible to mention the word "degrees" regarding the people of the Fire, when it has come in a report: "The Garden has degrees and the Fire has levels"? We say: there are several answers. The first: it is permissible to say that by way of predominance (taghlīb). The second: Ibn Zayd said: the degrees of the people of the Garden go upward, and the degrees of the people of the Fire go downward. The third: the intended meaning of "degrees" is increasing ranks, except that the increases of the people of the Garden are in good deeds and acts of obedience, and the increases of the people of the Fire are in sins and misdeeds.

* * *

Then God said: ﴿that He may fully compensate them﴾, and it has been read with nūn. This is a causal clause whose cause is omitted, as the context indicates, as if it meant: "that He may fully compensate them for their deeds and not wrong them their rights; He appointed their recompense according to the measure of their deeds, so He made rewards degrees and punishments levels." Since God explained that He delivers each person's right to him, He first explained the condition of the people of punishment, saying: ﴿And on the Day those who disbelieved are exposed to the Fire﴾. It was said: they enter the Fire; and it was said: the Fire is presented to them so that they may see its terrors. ﴿"You squandered your good things in your worldly life﴾. Ibn Kathīr read "ādhhabtum" as an interrogative with a hamzah and a madd; Ibn ʿĀmir read it as an interrogative with two hamzahs without a madd; and the rest read "adhhabtum" in the form of a declarative statement. The meaning is that everything that was decreed for you of good things and comforts you have fully received in this world and taken, so nothing of them remains for you after you have exhausted your portion. It is reported from ʿUmar: "Were I to wish, I would be the best of you in food and the finest of you in clothing, but I hold back my good things." And it is reported from the Messenger of God ﴿ﷺ﴾ that he entered upon the People of the Bench (Ahl al-Ṣuffah) while they were patching their clothes with leather, having no patches for them, and he said: "Are you today better, or the day when one of you goes out in one garment and comes back in another, and a bowl is brought to him in the morning and another in the evening, and his house is covered as the Kaʿbah is covered?" They said: "We were better on that day." He said: "Rather, you are better today." Reported by the author of al-Kashshāf. Al-Wāḥidī said: righteous people prefer asceticism and renunciation of the world, hoping that their reward in the Hereafter will be more complete. However, this verse does not indicate prohibition of enjoying comforts, because this verse was revealed concerning the disbeliever, and God rebuked the disbeliever because he enjoys the world without rendering thanks to the Benefactor through obedience and faith in Him. As for the believer, he renders the Benefactor's thanks through his faith, so he is not rebuked for enjoying. The proof of this is His saying: ﴿Say: Who has forbidden the adornment of God which He brought forth for His servants, and the good things of provision?﴾ [al-A‘rāf: 32]. Yes, it is not denied that abstaining from luxury is more preferable, because when the soul becomes accustomed to luxury, restraint and withdrawal become difficult for it; then its inclination toward those good things may lead it to do what is not fitting, and some of that draws it to other things, and it falls into distance from God Exalted because of it.

* * *

Then God said: ﴿So today you will be recompensed with the punishment of humiliation﴾, i.e., ʿadhāb al-hawn, meaning the disgrace. It has been read "ʿadhāb al-hawān."

﴿for what you were arrogant about in the earth without right and for what you used to defy.﴾ Here God gave a reason for that punishment with two matters:

The first: arrogance and haughtiness, which is a sin of the heart.

The second: defiance (fisq), which is a sin of the limbs. He placed the first before the second because states of the heart have a greater impact than deeds of the limbs. It is possible that by arrogance is meant that they were proud to accept the true religion, and disdained to believe in Muhammad, upon him be blessings and peace. As for defiance, it means sins. Our companions used this verse to argue that disbelievers are addressed with the branches of the sacred law. They said: since God gave a reason for their punishment with two matters: the first being disbelief, and the second being defiance, and this defiance must necessarily be distinct from that disbelief, because conjunction requires distinction. Therefore it is established that the defiance of the disbelievers makes punishment obligatory for them, and defiance has no meaning except abandoning what is commanded and doing what is forbidden. And God knows best.

The Exalted said: ﴿And he who says to his parents, "Uff to you both! Do you threaten me that I will be brought forth, when generations have passed before me?" * * *

Then He said: ﴿that I will be brought forth﴾, i.e., that I will be raised and brought out from the earth. It has been read "akhruja", and "when generations have passed before me", meaning that none of them has been raised.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿While they both call upon God for help﴾, i.e., the two parents call upon God for help. If they say: should it not have been said "yastaghīthāni bi-llāh" (call upon God for help)? We reply: the answer is in two respects:

The second: it is permissible to say the bāʾ was omitted, because by "istighāthah" is meant here supplication, as the exegetes said: "they both call upon God." Since supplication is intended by istighāthah, the preposition was omitted, because supplication does not require it. As for the believer, he renders the Benefactor's thanks through his faith, so he is not rebuked for enjoying. The proof of this is His saying: ﴿Say: Who has forbidden the adornment of God which He brought forth for His servants, and the good things of provision?﴾ [al-A‘rāf: 32]. Yes, it is not denied that abstaining from luxury is more preferable, because when the soul becomes accustomed to luxury, restraint and withdrawal become difficult for it; then its inclination toward those good things may lead it to do what is not fitting, and some of that draws it to other things, and it falls into distance from God Exalted because of it.

* * *

Then God said: ﴿So today you will be recompensed with the punishment of humiliation﴾, i.e., ʿadhāb al-hawn, meaning the disgrace. It has been read "ʿadhāb al-hawān."

﴿for what you were arrogant about in the earth without right and for what you used to defy.﴾ Here God gave a reason for that punishment with two matters:

The first: arrogance and haughtiness, which is a sin of the heart.

The second: defiance (fisq), which is a sin of the limbs. He placed the first before the second because states of the heart have a greater impact than deeds of the limbs. It is possible that by arrogance is meant that they were proud to accept the true religion, and disdained to believe in Muhammad, upon him be blessings and peace. As for defiance, it means sins. Our companions used this verse to argue that disbelievers are addressed with the branches of the sacred law. They said: since God gave a reason for their punishment with two matters: the first being disbelief, and the second being defiance, and this defiance must necessarily be distinct from that disbelief, because conjunction requires distinction. Therefore it is established that the defiance of the disbelievers makes punishment obligatory for them, and defiance has no meaning except abandoning what is commanded and doing what is forbidden. And God knows best.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 46, verses 21–26:

﴿And mention the brother of ʿAd, when he warned his people in al-Ahqaf (the winding sand-dunes), and warnings had passed before him and after him, saying: "Worship none but Allah; indeed I fear for you the punishment of a tremendous day."﴾ ﴿They said: "Have you come to us to turn us away from our gods? Then bring us what you threaten us with, if you are among the truthful."﴾ ﴿He said: "The knowledge is only with Allah. I convey to you what I have been sent with, but I see you as a people who are ignorant."﴾ ﴿Then when they saw it as a cloud coming towards their valleys, they said: "This is a cloud bringing us rain." Rather, it is what you were hastening: a wind in which is a painful punishment,﴾ ﴿destroying everything by the command of its Lord, so that they became such that nothing could be seen except their dwellings. Thus do We recompense the criminal people.﴾ ﴿And We had established them in that which We have not established you in, and We made for them hearing, sight and hearts, but their hearing, their sight and their hearts did not avail them anything, since they had been denying the signs of Allah; and there encompassed them what they had been mocking.﴾

Know that when Allah had presented the kinds of proofs for establishing monotheism (tawhid) and prophethood (nubuwwah), and the people of Makkah, because of their absorption in the pleasures of this world and their preoccupation with seeking them, turned away from these proofs and paid them no attention, for this reason Allah the Exalted said concerning them: ﴿On the Day when those who disbelieved are exposed to the Fire: "You squandered your good things in your worldly life"﴾. So when the matter was as such, He made clear that the people of ʿAd had been greater than them in wealth, strength and status, then Allah the Exalted sent down punishment upon them because of the evil consequence of their disbelief. So He mentioned this story here,

[Page 24]

so that the people of Makkah might take a lesson from it, abandon being deceived by what they had found of the world, and turn to seeking the religion. For this meaning, Allah the Exalted mentioned this story in this place, and it is suitable to what came before it, because whoever wants to denounce a way of behaviour among a people, the method is to strike examples, and the sense is: whoever persists in that way, such and such a calamity will befall him.

As for His saying ﴿and mention the brother of ʿAd﴾, meaning: and mention, O Muhammad, to your people, the people of Makkah, Hud (peace be upon him): ﴿when he warned his people﴾, meaning he warned them of the punishment of Allah if they did not believe. As for His saying ﴿in al-Ahqaf﴾, Abu ʿUbaydah said: the ḥiqf is the winding sand, and from it the winding thing is called maḥquf. Al-Farra' said: al-Ahqaf is the plural of ḥiqf, which is a broken sand-hill that is not large and has a curve in it. Ibn ʿAbbas said: "al-Ahqaf" is a valley between ʿUman and Mahrah. And "al-nudhur" is the plural of nadhir in the sense of mundhir (warner). ﴿from before him﴾ means from his time, ﴿and from after him﴾ means after him. The meaning is: Hud (peace be upon him) had warned them and said to them: ﴿that you worship none but Allah; indeed I fear for you the punishment of a tremendous day﴾.

Know that the messengers who were sent before him and those who will be sent after him are all warners in the manner of his warning.

Then the Exalted related about the disbelievers that they said: ﴿Have you come to us to turn us away?﴾ The ifk (turning away) is diversion; it is said: "afakahu ʿan raʾyihi", meaning he diverted him from his opinion. It was also said: the meaning is "to remove us by some kind of falsehood" ﴿from our gods﴾ and from worshipping them. ﴿Then bring us what you threaten us with﴾ meaning hastening the punishment for shirk ﴿if you are among the truthful﴾ in your promise. At this, Hud said: ﴿The knowledge is only with Allah﴾. This speech is suitable as a reply to their words ﴿bring us what you threaten us with﴾, because their saying ﴿bring us what you threaten us with﴾ was a demand from them for that punishment, so Hud said to them: I have no knowledge of the time at which that punishment will occur; the knowledge of that is only with Allah the Exalted. ﴿And I convey to you what I have been sent with﴾, which is the warning of the punishment, but as for knowledge of its time, Allah has not revealed it to me. ﴿But I see you as a people who are ignorant﴾. This has several possible meanings:

First: the meaning is that you do not know that the messengers were not sent to ask about what they were not permitted to, but were sent only as conveyors.

Second: "I see you as a people who are ignorant" in that you remain persistent in your disbelief and ignorance, so it is strongly my assumption that the time is near at which the punishment will descend upon you, because of this extreme ignorance and complete audacity.

Third: "I see you as a people who are ignorant" in that you insist on demanding the punishment; and suppose it did not become apparent to you that I am truthful, yet it has also not become apparent to you that I am lying; so rushing vehemently to demand this punishment is great ignorance.

* * *

Then the Exalted said: ﴿Then when they saw it﴾. Al-Mubarrad mentioned two views regarding the pronoun in "ra'awhu" (they saw it). The first: it refers to something not mentioned, which is clarified by His saying ﴿as a cloud﴾, just as He said: ﴿He left on its back no creature﴾ [Fatir: 45], and He did not mention the earth because it is known; likewise here the pronoun refers to the clouds, as if it were said: "when they saw the clouds as a cloud coming towards them." This is the choice of al-Zajjaj, and it is of the type of implicit reference (idmar) not under the condition of explanation (tafsir).

The second view: the pronoun refers to what is in His saying ﴿bring us what you threaten us with﴾, meaning: when they saw what they were threatened with as a cloud. Abu Zayd said: ʿaridh is the cloud seen in a side of the sky, then it spreads over. As for His saying ﴿coming towards their valleys﴾, the exegetes said: ʿAd had been withheld from rain for days, so Allah drove to them a black cloud, and it came out over them from a valley called al-Mughith. When they saw it coming towards their valleys, they rejoiced and ﴿said: "This is a cloud bringing us rain"﴾, and the meaning is "bringing rain to us". It was said that Hud was sitting among his people when a heavy cloud came, and they said: "This is a cloud bringing us rain". He said: ﴿Rather, it is what you were hastening﴾ of the punishment; then he clarified its reality, saying: ﴿a wind in which is a painful punishment﴾. Then he described that wind, saying: ﴿destroying everything﴾, meaning destroying everything of the people, animals and plants ﴿by the command of its Lord﴾. The meaning is that this is not of the type of influences of the stars and conjunctions, but is a matter that came into being from the beginning by the power of Allah the Exalted for the purpose of punishing you.

[Page 25]

﴿So they became such that nothing could be seen except their dwellings﴾, meaning ʿAd. On this there are several issues:

First issue: It is related that the wind would carry the tent and lift it into the air until it appeared like a locust. It was said: the first of them to see the punishment was a woman who said: "I saw a wind in which were like sparks of fire." It is also related that the first thing by which they knew that it was a painful punishment was that they saw what was in the desert of their men and livestock being carried by the wind between heaven and earth. So they entered their houses and locked their doors, but the wind lifted the doors and threw them down. Allah made the sand-dunes (al-Ahqaf) fall upon them, so they were beneath them for seven nights and eight days, moaning. Then the wind lifted away from them, carried them off and threw them into the sea. It is related that when Hud sensed the wind, he drew a line around himself and the believers, next to a spring that flowed, so the wind that struck them was a gentle, calm and pleasant wind, while the wind that struck the people of ʿAd lifted them from the ground, sent them flying into the sky, and dashed them on the ground. The effect of the miracle appeared in that wind from this aspect. It is related from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "Allah did not command the keeper of the winds to send upon ʿAd except an amount equal to the size of a ring." Then that amount destroyed them entirely. The purpose of this statement is to show the perfection of Allah's power. It is related from the Prophet (ﷺ) that when he saw the wind he would be alarmed and say: "O Allah, I ask You for its good and the good of what it was sent with, and I seek refuge in You from its evil and the evil of what it was sent with."

Third issue: ʿAsim and Hamzah recited "lā yurā" with a ya' and with a damma, "masākinuhum" with a damma on the nun. Al-Kisa'i said: its meaning is "nothing can be seen except their dwellings." Nafi', Ibn Kathir, Abu ʿAmr, Ibn ʿAmir and al-Kisa'i recited "lā narā" (we do not see), in the address form, meaning "you, the one addressed, do not see." In some narrations from ʿAsim it is "lā turā" with a ta', "masākinuhum" with a damma on the nun, and this is the recitation (qira'ah) of al-Hasan. The interpretation: "nothing of the remnants of ʿAd is seen except their dwellings." The majority said this recitation is not strong.

* * *

Then the Exalted said: ﴿Thus do We recompense the criminal people﴾. The purpose of this is to frighten the disbelievers of Makkah. If it is said: since Allah said ﴿And Allah would not punish them while you are among them﴾, how then does the fear remain effective? We say: His saying ﴿And Allah would not punish them while you are among them﴾ was revealed only at the end of the matter, so the fear was effective before its revelation.

Then He the Exalted warned the disbelievers of Makkah, and mentioned the superiority of ʿAd over them in strength and physique, so He said: ﴿And We had established them in that in which We have not established you﴾. Al-Mubarrad said: "ma" in His saying "fīmā" is in the position of "alladhī" (that which), and "in" is in the position of "mā" (not), and the sense is: "We had established them in that which We did not establish you in", and the meaning is that they were stronger than you in power and greater than you in wealth. Ibn Qutaybah said: the word "in" is superfluous, and the sense is: "We had established them in that in which We established you", and this is an error for several reasons:

First: that the judgment that a particle of the Book of Allah is futile is something no sensible person holds.

Second: the purpose of this statement is that they were stronger than you in power, and then despite their greater power they were not saved from the punishment of Allah, so how will your condition be? This purpose is only complete if the verse indicates that they were stronger than the people of Makkah.

Third: other verses convey this meaning. He the Exalted said: ﴿they had better furniture﴾ [Maryam: 74], and He said: ﴿They were more numerous than them, and stronger in power, and greater in remains in the earth﴾ [Ghafir: 82].

* * *

Then He the Exalted said: ﴿And We made for them hearing, sight and hearts﴾. The meaning is that We opened for them the doors of blessings and gave them hearing, but they did not use it to listen to the proofs; We gave them sight, but they did not use it to reflect upon lessons; We gave them hearts, but they did not use them to seek knowledge of Allah the Exalted. Rather they directed all these faculties to seeking the world and its pleasures. So, inevitably, their hearing, their sight and their hearts did not avail them anything against the punishment of Allah.

[Page 26]

Then the Exalted made clear that the reason their hearing, their sight and their hearts did not avail them was that they were denying the signs of Allah. His saying ﴿since they had been denying﴾ is in the sense of causation, and the word "idh" is sometimes mentioned to indicate causation. You say: "I struck him since he did wrong", meaning "I struck him because he did wrong." In this verse there is a warning to the people of Makkah, for when the people of ʿAd were deceived by their worldly life and turned away from accepting proof and argument, the punishment of Allah descended upon them, and their strength and their numbers did not avail them. So the people of Makkah, despite their weakness and feebleness, are more deserving of being wary of the punishment of Allah the Exalted and fearing it.

* * *

Then the Exalted said: ﴿And there encompassed them what they had been mocking﴾. This means that they had been asking for the punishment to descend, but they were only asking for it by way of mockery. And Allah knows best.

As for His saying ﴿coming towards their valleys﴾, the exegetes said: ʿAd had been withheld from rain for days, so Allah drove to them a black cloud, and it came out over them from a valley called al-Mughith. When they saw it coming towards their valleys, they rejoiced and ﴿said: "This is a cloud bringing us rain"﴾, and the meaning is "bringing rain to us". It was said that Hud was sitting among his people when a heavy cloud came, and they said: "This is a cloud bringing us rain". Then he described that wind, saying: ﴿destroying everything﴾, meaning destroying everything of the people, animals and plants ﴿by the command of its Lord﴾. [Page 25]

﴿So they became such that nothing could be seen except their dwellings﴾, meaning ʿAd. On this there are several issues:

First issue: It is related that the wind would carry the tent and lift it into the air until it appeared like a locust. It was said: the first of them to see the punishment was a woman who said: "I saw a wind in which were like sparks of fire." It is also related that the first thing by which they knew that it was a painful punishment was that they saw what was in the desert of their men and livestock being carried by the wind between heaven and earth. So they entered their houses and locked their doors, but the wind lifted the doors and threw them down. Allah made the sand-dunes (al-Ahqaf) fall upon them, so they were beneath them for seven nights and eight days, moaning. Then the wind lifted away from them, carried them off and threw them into the sea. It is related that when Hud sensed the wind, he drew a line around himself and the believers, next to a spring that flowed, so the wind that struck them was a gentle, calm and pleasant wind, while the wind that struck the people of ʿAd lifted them from the ground, sent them flying into the sky, and dashed them on the ground. The effect of the miracle appeared in that wind from this aspect. It is related from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "Allah did not command the keeper of the winds to send upon ʿAd except an amount equal to the size of a ring." Then that amount destroyed them entirely. The purpose of this statement is to show the perfection of Allah's power. It is related from the Prophet (ﷺ) that when he saw the wind he would be alarmed and say: "O Allah, I ask You for its good and the good of what it was sent with, and I seek refuge in You from its evil and the evil of what it was sent with."

* * *

Then the Exalted said: ﴿Thus do We recompense the criminal people﴾. The purpose of this is to frighten the disbelievers of Makkah. If it is said: since Allah said ﴿And Allah would not punish them while you are among them﴾, how then does the fear remain effective? We say: His saying ﴿And Allah would not punish them while you are among them﴾ was revealed only at the end of the matter, so the fear was effective before its revelation.

Then He the Exalted warned the disbelievers of Makkah, and mentioned the superiority of ʿAd over them in strength and physique, so He said: ﴿And We had established them in that in which We have not established you﴾. Al-Mubarrad said: "ma" in His saying "fīmā" is in the position of "alladhī" (that which), and "in" is in the position of "mā" (not), and the sense is: "We had established them in that which We did not establish you in", and the meaning is that they were stronger than you in power and greater than you in wealth. Third: other verses convey this meaning. He the Exalted said: ﴿they had better furniture﴾ [Maryam: 74], and He said: ﴿They were more numerous than them, and stronger in power, and greater in remains in the earth﴾ [Ghafir: 82].

The meaning is that We opened for them the doors of blessings and gave them hearing, but they did not use it to listen to the proofs; We gave them sight, but they did not use it to reflect upon lessons; We gave them hearts, but they did not use them to seek knowledge of Allah the Exalted. Rather they directed all these faculties to seeking the world and its pleasures. So, inevitably, their hearing, their sight and their hearts did not avail them anything against the punishment of Allah.

[Page 26]

Then the Exalted made clear that the reason their hearing, their sight and their hearts did not avail them was that they were denying the signs of Allah. Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 46, verses 21–26:

﴿And mention the brother of ʿAd, when he warned his people in al-Ahqaf (the winding sand-dunes), and warnings had passed before him and after him, saying: "Worship none but Allah; indeed I fear for you the punishment of a tremendous day."﴾ ﴿They said: "Have you come to us to turn us away from our gods? Then bring us what you threaten us with, if you are among the truthful."﴾ ﴿He said: "The knowledge is only with Allah. I convey to you what I have been sent with, but I see you as a people who are ignorant."﴾ ﴿Then when they saw it as a cloud coming towards their valleys, they said: "This is a cloud bringing us rain." Rather, it is what you were hastening: a wind in which is a painful punishment,﴾ ﴿destroying everything by the command of its Lord, so that they became such that nothing could be seen except their dwellings. Thus do We recompense the criminal people.﴾ ﴿And We had established them in that which We have not established you in, and We made for them hearing, sight and hearts, but their hearing, their sight and their hearts did not avail them anything, since they had been denying the signs of Allah; and there encompassed them what they had been mocking.﴾

Know that when Allah had presented the kinds of proofs for establishing monotheism (tawhid) and prophethood (nubuwwah), and the people of Makkah, because of their absorption in the pleasures of this world and their preoccupation with seeking them, turned away from these proofs and paid them no attention, for this reason Allah the Exalted said concerning them: ﴿On the Day when those who disbelieved are exposed to the Fire: "You squandered your good things in your worldly life"﴾. So when the matter was as such, He made clear that the people of ʿAd had been greater than them in wealth, strength and status, then Allah the Exalted sent down punishment upon them because of the evil consequence of their disbelief. So He mentioned this story here,

so that the people of Makkah might take a lesson from it, abandon being deceived by what they had found of the world, and turn to seeking the religion. For this meaning, Allah the Exalted mentioned this story in this place, and it is suitable to what came before it, because whoever wants to denounce a way of behaviour among a people, the method is to strike examples, and the sense is: whoever persists in that way, such and such a calamity will befall him.

As for His saying ﴿in al-Ahqaf﴾, Abu ʿUbaydah said: the ḥiqf is the winding sand, and from it the winding thing is called maḥquf. Al-Farra' said: al-Ahqaf is the plural of ḥiqf, which is a broken sand-hill that is not large and has a curve in it. Ibn ʿAbbas said: "al-Ahqaf" is a valley between ʿUman and Mahrah. And "al-nudhur" is the plural of nadhir in the sense of mundhir (warner). ﴿from before him﴾ means from his time, ﴿and from after him﴾ means after him. The meaning is: Hud (peace be upon him) had warned them and said to them: ﴿that you worship none but Allah; indeed I fear for you the punishment of a tremendous day﴾.

This speech is suitable as a reply to their words ﴿bring us what you threaten us with﴾, because their saying ﴿bring us what you threaten us with﴾ was a demand from them for that punishment, so Hud said to them: I have no knowledge of the time at which that punishment will occur; the knowledge of that is only with Allah the Exalted. ﴿And I convey to you what I have been sent with﴾, which is the warning of the punishment, but as for knowledge of its time, Allah has not revealed it to me. ﴿But I see you as a people who are ignorant﴾.
