Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 46, verses 27–28:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We had destroyed what was around you of the towns, and We had varied the signs that they might return.﴾ ﴿Why then did those whom they had taken as gods besides Allah, as a means of nearness, not help them? Rather they went astray from them. That was their falsehood, and what they used to fabricate.﴾

Know that the intended meaning is: "And We had destroyed what was around you, O disbelievers of Makkah, of the towns, and they are the towns of ʿAd and Thamud in Yemen and al-Sham." ﴿And We varied the signs﴾, i.e., We made them clear to them. "That they might" (laʿallahum), i.e., that the people of the towns might "return." So by the "variation" is meant the terrifying circumstances that occurred before the destruction. Al-Jubba'i said: His saying ﴿that they might return﴾ means "in order that they might return from their disbelief," which indicates that He, exalted is He, willed their return and did not will their persistence. The answer: He did what, if anyone else had done it, would have been for the sake of the aforementioned will. We only went to this interpretation because of the proofs indicating that He, glorified is He, wills all existing things.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Why then did those whom they had taken as gods besides Allah, as a means of nearness, not help them?﴾ Qurban is that by which one draws near to Allah, exalted is He; that is, they took them as intercessors through whom they drew near to Allah, as they said: ﴿These are our intercessors with Allah﴾ [Yunus: 18], and they said: ﴿We only worship them so that they may bring us near to Allah in nearness﴾ [al-Zumar: 3]. As for the grammatical analysis (i'rab) of the verse, there are several views:

The first: The author of al-Kashshaf said: one of the two objects of "took" (ittakhadha), namely the pronoun referring back to "those," is omitted.

The second: "Gods" (alihatan) and "as a means of nearness" (qurbanan) are a circumstantial clause (hal). It was objected to this that a verb transitive to two objects is not complete except by mentioning both of them explicitly, and a circumstantial clause indicates the completion of the sentence; and there is no doubt that placing the circumstantial clause between the two objects contradicts the original arrangement.

The third: Some said: "as a means of nearness" (qurbanan) is the second object, placed before the first object, which is "gods" (alihatan). It was objected to this that it leads to the sentence being devoid of the pronoun referring back to "those."

The fourth: Some of the verifiers (muhaqqiqin) said: one of the two objects of "they took" is omitted, namely the pronoun referring back to "those," and "as a means of nearness" (qurbanan) is made the second object, while "gods" (alihatan) is an explicative apposition (ʿatf bayan). Once you know the discussion of the grammar, we say: the intended meaning is that when those whom Allah destroyed, why did those who worshipped them not help them, and they claimed that by worshipping them they drew near to Allah so that they would intercede for them? ﴿Rather they went astray from them﴾, i.e., they were absent from their help. "That" is an indication that the fact that their gods were helpers to them is an impossible matter.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿That was their falsehood﴾, i.e., that impossibility is the result of their falsehood, which is their taking them as gods, and the fruit of their polytheism and their fabrication against Allah, the lie in affirming partners for Him. The author of al-Kashshaf said: it has been read as "ifkuhum," and "al-ifk" and "al-afk" are like "al-hidhr" and "al-hadhr." It has also been read as "wa-dhalika afakahum," with a fatha on the fa and the kaf, i.e., that taking, whose result and fruit is this, turned them away from the truth. It has also been read as "affakahum" with shadda for emphasis (mubalaghah): "affakahum" made them ones who lie (afikin), and "afakuhum," i.e., their saying of falsehood (al-ifk), i.e., possessors of falsehood, just as you say "a false saying" (qawl kadhib).

* * *

Then He said: ﴿and what they used to fabricate﴾. The estimated meaning is: "That was their falsehood and their fabrication in affirming partners to Allah, exalted is He." And Allah knows best.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And [mention] when We turned towards you a group of the jinn, listening to the Qur'an. When they attended it, they said, "Be silent." When he returned to Makkah, and was in the Valley of Nakhla, he stood reciting the Qur'an in the dawn prayer. A group of the noble jinn of Nasibin passed by him, for Iblis had sent them to learn the reason that had made the guarding of the sky with pelting necessary. They heard the Qur'an and realized that this was the cause.

**The second branch:** The author of *al-Kashshaf* said: *al-nafar* is fewer than ten, and its plural is *anfar*. Then Muhammad ibn Jarir al-Tabari narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that those jinn were seven men from the people of Nasibin, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ made them messengers to their people. And from Zirr ibn Hubaysh: they were nine, one of whom was Zawba'a. And from Qatadah: it was mentioned to us that they were turned towards him from Sawa.

[p. 28]

**The third branch:** They differed as to whether 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud was with the Prophet ﷺ on the night of the jinn. The reports on this are varied and well known.

**The fourth branch:** al-Qadi narrated in his commentary, on the authority of Anas, who said: "I was with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ in the mountains of Makkah when an old man approached, leaning on a staff. The Prophet ﷺ said: 'A jinni's gait and his voice.' He said: 'Indeed.' He said: 'Which of the jinn are you?' He said: 'I am Hamah ibn Haym ibn Laqis ibn Iblis.' He said: 'I see no more than two fathers between you and Iblis. How long has passed over you?' He said: 'I have eaten the life of this world except its least part, and at the time Qabil killed Habil I was walking among the hills.' He mentioned much of what he had passed through, and among what he mentioned he said: 'Jesus son of Mary said to me: If you meet Muhammad, convey my greetings to him. **The second issue:** They differed in the interpretation of His saying: ﴿And when We turned towards you a group of the jinn﴾. Some of them said: Since the Messenger ﷺ did not intend to recite the Qur'an to them, He the Exalted placed in their hearts an inclination and a call to listen to the Qur'an. For this reason He said: ﴿And when We turned towards you a group of the jinn﴾.

* * *

Then the Exalted said: ﴿When they attended it﴾, the pronoun refers either to the Qur'an or to the Messenger of Allah. ﴿They said﴾, meaning some of them said to others: ﴿Be silent﴾, meaning: be quiet while listening. It is said: *anṣata* for such-and-such, and *istanṣata lahu*. ﴿When it was concluded﴾, meaning when the recitation finished, ﴿they went back to their people as warners﴾, warning them. This could only happen after their belief, for they would not call others to listen to the Qur'an and to believe in it unless they had themselves believed. Thereupon: ﴿They said, "O our people, we have heard a Book revealed after Moses"﴾, and they described it with two attributes:

The first: that it is ﴿confirming what came before it﴾, meaning confirming the books of the prophets. The meaning is that the books of all the prophets contained the call to monotheism, prophethood, the return [to Allah], and the command to purify character; likewise this Book contains these meanings.

The second: His saying: ﴿guiding to the truth and to a straight path﴾.

Know that the first attribute indicates that this Book resembles all the divine books in calling to these lofty and noble matters. The second attribute indicates that these matters which the Qur'an contains are true and genuine in themselves, and every person knows by the plain testimony of his intellect that they are so, whether or not divine books had come with them before. If someone says: How could they say ﴿after Moses﴾? We say: al-Hasan has transmitted that they were upon Judaism, and Ibn 'Abbas [transmitted] that the jinn had not heard of the command of Jesus, and therefore they said: ﴿after Moses﴾. Then, when the jinn had described the Qur'an with these excellent attributes, they said: ﴿O our people, respond to the summoner of Allah﴾. They differed as to whether by "the summoner of Allah" is meant the Messenger, or the intermediary who conveys from Him. The closer view is that it is the Messenger, because he is the one to whom this description is applied.

**The first issue:** This verse indicates that he ﷺ was sent to the jinn just as he was sent to mankind. Muqatil said: Allah had not sent any prophet to mankind and the jinn before him.

However, He repeated the mention of belief specifically, because it is the most important and noblest of its categories. It is the custom of the Qur'an to mention a general term and then add its noblest kinds, as in His saying: ﴿and His angels and His messengers and Gabriel﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:98], and His saying: ﴿And when We took from the prophets their covenant, and from you, and from Noah﴾ [al-Ahzab 33:7]. **The first issue:** Some said: The word "min" (from) here is superfluous, and the sense is "He will forgive you your sins." It was also said: Rather, the benefit of it is that the word "min" here denotes the starting point, so the meaning is that the forgiveness of sins begins from the sins and then extends to the forgiveness of what proceeds from you of leaving the better and the more perfect.

**The second issue:** They differed as to whether the jinn have reward or not. And when it was concluded, they went back to their people as warners.﴾ ﴿They said, "O our people, we have heard a Book revealed after Moses, confirming what came before it, guiding to the truth and to a straight path."﴾ ﴿O our people, respond to the summoner of Allah and believe in him; He will forgive you your sins and protect you from a painful punishment.﴾ ﴿And whoever does not respond to the summoner of Allah will not escape [Him] on earth, and he will have no protectors other than Him. Those are in manifest error.﴾

In the verse there are several issues.

**The first issue:** Know that when Allah the Exalted had explained that among mankind there are those who believe and those who disbelieve, He also explained that among the jinn there are those who believe and those who disbelieve. Their believers are exposed to reward, and their disbelievers are exposed to punishment. Regarding the manner of this event there are two opinions.

The first: Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: The jinn used to eavesdrop, but when they were pelted [with meteors], they said, "This that has happened in the sky must have happened for something on earth," so they went seeking the cause. It so happened that the Prophet ﷺ, when he despaired of the people of Makkah responding to him, went out to Ta'if to call them to Islam. When he returned to Makkah, and was in the Valley of Nakhla, he stood reciting the Qur'an in the dawn prayer. A group of the noble jinn of Nasibin passed by him, for Iblis had sent them to learn the reason that had made the guarding of the sky with pelting necessary. They heard the Qur'an and realized that this was the cause.

The second opinion: Allah the Exalted commanded His Messenger to warn the jinn, to call them to Allah the Exalted, and to recite the Qur'an to them. So Allah turned towards him a group of the jinn so that they might listen to the Qur'an from him and warn their people.

Several branches follow from what we have mentioned:

**The first branch:** It is reported from al-Qadi in his commentary on the jinn that he said: They were Jews, because among the jinn there are religious communities just as among mankind there are Jews, Christians, Magians, and idol-worshippers. The scholars have agreed that the jinn are morally accountable. Ibn 'Abbas was asked: "Do the jinn have reward?" He said: "Yes, they have reward and they have punishment. They will meet in Paradise and crowd at its gates."

**The second branch:** The author of *al-Kashshaf* said: *al-nafar* is fewer than ten, and its plural is *anfar*. Then Muhammad ibn Jarir al-Tabari narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that those jinn were seven men from the people of Nasibin, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ made them messengers to their people. And from Zirr ibn Hubaysh: they were nine, one of whom was Zawba'a. And from Qatadah: it was mentioned to us that they were turned towards him from Sawa.

[p. 28]

**The third branch:** They differed as to whether 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud was with the Prophet ﷺ on the night of the jinn. The reports on this are varied and well known.

**The fourth branch:** al-Qadi narrated in his commentary, on the authority of Anas, who said: "I was with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ in the mountains of Makkah when an old man approached, leaning on a staff. The Prophet ﷺ said: 'A jinni's gait and his voice.' He said: 'Indeed.' He said: 'Which of the jinn are you?' He said: 'I am Hamah ibn Haym ibn Laqis ibn Iblis.' He said: 'I see no more than two fathers between you and Iblis. How long has passed over you?' He said: 'I have eaten the life of this world except its least part, and at the time Qabil killed Habil I was walking among the hills.' He mentioned much of what he had passed through, and among what he mentioned he said: 'Jesus son of Mary said to me: If you meet Muhammad, convey my greetings to him. I have conveyed his greeting and I believed in you.' He ﷺ said: 'And upon Jesus be peace, and upon you, O Hamah. What is your need?' He said: 'Moses, peace be upon him, taught me the Torah, and Jesus taught me the Gospel, so teach me the Qur'an.' So he taught him ten surahs. And [the old man] remained until the Prophet ﷺ passed away, and he did not die [before that]." 'Umar ibn al-Khattab said: "I do not think he is anything but alive." Know that the complete discussion of the story of the jinn is mentioned in Surah al-Jinn.

**The second issue:** They differed in the interpretation of His saying: ﴿And when We turned towards you a group of the jinn﴾. Some of them said: Since the Messenger ﷺ did not intend to recite the Qur'an to them, He the Exalted placed in their hearts an inclination and a call to listen to the Qur'an. For this reason He said: ﴿And when We turned towards you a group of the jinn﴾.

* * *

Then the Exalted said: ﴿When they attended it﴾, the pronoun refers either to the Qur'an or to the Messenger of Allah. ﴿They said﴾, meaning some of them said to others: ﴿Be silent﴾, meaning: be quiet while listening. It is said: *anṣata* for such-and-such, and *istanṣata lahu*. ﴿When it was concluded﴾, meaning when the recitation finished, ﴿they went back to their people as warners﴾, warning them. This could only happen after their belief, for they would not call others to listen to the Qur'an and to believe in it unless they had themselves believed. Thereupon: ﴿They said, "O our people, we have heard a Book revealed after Moses"﴾, and they described it with two attributes:

The first: that it is ﴿confirming what came before it﴾, meaning confirming the books of the prophets. The meaning is that the books of all the prophets contained the call to monotheism, prophethood, the return [to Allah], and the command to purify character; likewise this Book contains these meanings.

The second: His saying: ﴿guiding to the truth and to a straight path﴾.

Know that the first attribute indicates that this Book resembles all the divine books in calling to these lofty and noble matters. The second attribute indicates that these matters which the Qur'an contains are true and genuine in themselves, and every person knows by the plain testimony of his intellect that they are so, whether or not divine books had come with them before. If someone says: How could they say ﴿after Moses﴾? We say: al-Hasan has transmitted that they were upon Judaism, and Ibn 'Abbas [transmitted] that the jinn had not heard of the command of Jesus, and therefore they said: ﴿after Moses﴾. Then, when the jinn had described the Qur'an with these excellent attributes, they said: ﴿O our people, respond to the summoner of Allah﴾. They differed as to whether by "the summoner of Allah" is meant the Messenger, or the intermediary who conveys from Him. The closer view is that it is the Messenger, because he is the one to whom this description is applied.

Know that His saying ﴿respond to the summoner of Allah﴾ contains two issues:

**The first issue:** This verse indicates that he ﷺ was sent to the jinn just as he was sent to mankind. Muqatil said: Allah had not sent any prophet to mankind and the jinn before him.

[p. 29]

**The second issue:** His saying ﴿respond to the summoner of Allah﴾ is a command to respond to him in everything he commands, so the command to believe is included in it. However, He repeated the mention of belief specifically, because it is the most important and noblest of its categories. It is the custom of the Qur'an to mention a general term and then add its noblest kinds, as in His saying: ﴿and His angels and His messengers and Gabriel﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:98], and His saying: ﴿And when We took from the prophets their covenant, and from you, and from Noah﴾ [al-Ahzab 33:7]. When He commanded belief in him, He mentioned the benefit of that belief, which is His saying: ﴿He will forgive you your sins﴾. Regarding this there are two issues:

**The first issue:** Some said: The word "min" (from) here is superfluous, and the sense is "He will forgive you your sins." It was also said: Rather, the benefit of it is that the word "min" here denotes the starting point, so the meaning is that the forgiveness of sins begins from the sins and then extends to the forgiveness of what proceeds from you of leaving the better and the more perfect.

**The second issue:** They differed as to whether the jinn have reward or not. It was said: They have no reward except salvation from the Fire, and then it will be said to them: "Be dust like the beasts." They argued for the soundness of this view by His saying the Exalted: ﴿and protect you from a painful punishment﴾. This is the view of Abu Hanifa. The correct view is that they are under the same ruling as the children of Adam, so they deserve reward for obedience and punishment for disobedience. This is the view of Ibn Abi Layla and Malik, and a debate took place between him and Abu Hanifa on this matter. al-Dahhak said: They enter Paradise and eat and drink. The evidence for the soundness of this view is that every proof which indicates that humans deserve reward for obedience applies in exactly the same way to the jinn, and the difference between the two cases is very remote.

Know that when that jinni commanded his people to respond to the Messenger and to believe in him, he warned them against that response, saying: ﴿And whoever does not respond to the summoner of Allah will not escape [Him] on earth﴾, meaning no refuge will save him from Him, and no one who has preceded His decree will outrun it. A parallel to this is His saying the Exalted: ﴿And we thought that we could never escape Allah on earth, nor could we escape Him by flight﴾ [al-Jinn 72:12]. ﴿And he will have no protectors other than Him﴾, nor any helper or defender apart from Allah. Then He explained that they are in manifest error.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb, *The Keys to the Unseen*) on Surah 46, verses 33–34:**

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Do they not see that God, who created the heavens and the earth and was not wearied by their creation, is able to give life to the dead? Yes, indeed He is Powerful over all things.﴾ ﴿On the Day when those who disbelieved are exposed to the Fire: "Is this not the truth?" They will say, "Yes, by our Lord." He will say, "So taste the punishment for what you used to disbelieve."﴾ Concerning this verse there are several issues:

**The first issue:** Know that at the beginning of the surah He mentioned what indicates the existence of the All-Powerful, Wise, Chooser God, and then He built two branches upon it. The first: refuting the saying of the idol-worshippers. The second: affirming prophethood, and He mentioned the doubts they raised against prophethood and answered them. Since most of the rejection by the disbelievers of Mecca of accepting the proofs was due to their being deceived by this world and their absorption in obtaining its good things and desires, and because it was burdensome for them to submit to Muhammad and acknowledge his precedence over them, He cited an example for that: the people of ʿAd. They had been more complete in the benefits of this world than the people of Muhammad. When they persisted in disbelief, God annihilated and destroyed them. This was a warning to the people of Mecca about their persistence in denying the prophethood of Muhammad, peace be upon him. Then, when He had established his prophethood over humankind, He followed it with affirming his prophethood over the jinn. Up to this point the discourse on monotheism (tawhid) and prophethood has been completed. Then He mentioned after these two the establishment of the question of the Return (al-maʿad, the afterlife). Whoever reflects on this explanation that we have mentioned will know that the purpose of the entire Qur'an is the establishment of monotheism, prophethood and the Return. As for the stories, the purpose of mentioning them is what serves the function of coining examples in establishing these principles.

**The second issue:** The aim of this verse is to establish the proof that He, exalted is He, is able to resurrect. The evidence for this is that He established proofs at the beginning of this surah that: ﴿It is He who created the heavens and the earth﴾. There is no doubt that creating them is greater and more magnificent than restoring this person to life after he has become dead. Whoever is able to do the stronger and more perfect is necessarily able to do the weaker and lesser. Then He concluded the verse with His saying: ﴿Indeed He is Powerful over all things﴾. What is meant by it is that the attachment of the soul to the body is something possible, for if it were not possible in itself, it would not have occurred in the first place. God, exalted is He, is capable of all possible things, so it is necessary that He be capable of that restoration. These proofs are certain and manifest.

**The third issue:** In His saying, exalted is He: ﴿bi-qadir﴾ (with a Powerful one), the bāʾ (with) is attached to the predicate of *inna* (indeed). The reason this is permissible is that the negative particle has entered upon *anna* (that) and what is connected to it. It is as if it were said: "Is God not Powerful?" Al-Zajjaj said: "If you say, *mā ẓanantu anna Zayden bi-qāʾimin* (I did not think that Zayd was standing), it is permissible. But it is not permissible to say *ẓanantu anna Zayden bi-qāʾimin* (I thought that Zayd was standing)." And God knows best.

**The fourth issue:** It is said: *ʿayiytu bi-l-amr* (I was unable to find the way through the matter) when you do not know its way. From it is His saying: ﴿Were We then wearied by the first creation?﴾ [Qaf: 15].

Know that when He, exalted is He, had established the proof for the correctness of the doctrine of the gathering and the dispersal (al-ḥashr wa-l-nashr), He mentioned some of the conditions of the disbelievers, so He said: ﴿On the Day when those who disbelieved are exposed to the Fire: "Is this not the truth?" They will say, "Yes, by our Lord." He will say, "So taste the punishment for what you used to disbelieve."﴾ His saying: ﴿Is this not the truth?﴾ has the implied meaning: "It will be said to them, 'Is this not the truth?'" The purpose is to mock them and to rebuke them for their ridiculing God's promise and threat, and their saying: ﴿We shall not be punished﴾ [al-Shuʿara: 138].

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 46, verse 35:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So be patient, as the steadfast of the messengers were patient, and do not seek to hasten [the punishment] for them. As for them, on the day they see what they are promised, it will be as though they had not remained [in the world] except for an hour of a day. [This is] a message. So will anyone be destroyed except the defiantly disobedient people?﴾.

Know that when the Exalted had established the three matters—Tawhid (Oneness of God), Prophethood, and the Return (ma'ad)—and had answered the doubts, He followed them with what amounts to admonition and advice to the Messenger ﷺ. This is because the disbelievers were harming him and troubling his heart. So the Exalted said: ﴿So be patient, as the steadfast of the messengers were patient﴾, meaning: those of resolve, endurance, and firmness. Regarding the verse there are two views:

The first: the word "min" (from) is partitive (lit-tab'id), and "ulu al-'azm" refers to some of the prophets. It has been said they are: Nuh, who was patient with the harm of his people, who would beat him until he fainted; Ibrahim, with the fire and the slaughter of his son; Ishaq, with the (threat of) slaughter; Ya'qub, with the loss of a son and the loss of his sight; Yusuf, with the well and the prison; Ayyub, with affliction; Musa, whose people said to him: ﴿Indeed, we are overtaken﴾ [al-Shu'ara’: 61], and he said: ﴿No! Indeed, with me is my Lord; He will guide me﴾ [al-Shu'ara’: 62]; Dawud, who wept over his lapse for forty years; and Isa, who did not place one brick upon another, and said: "Indeed, it is a passageway, so pass through it and do not build upon it." And the Exalted said about Adam: ﴿And We did not find in him resolve﴾ [Ta-Ha: 115], and about Yunus: ﴿And do not be like the companion of the fish﴾ [al-Qalam: 48].

The second view: all the messengers are "ulu al-'azm," for Allah did not send a messenger except that he was one of resolve and firmness, judgment, opinion, perfection, and intellect. The word "min" in His saying ﴿from the messengers﴾ is explicative (tabyin), not partitive, as one says: "I clothed him in khazz" (silk). It is as if it were said: "Be patient as the messengers before you were patient over the harm of their people," and He described them with resolve because of their patience and steadfastness.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿And do not seek to hasten [the punishment] for them﴾, and the object of "istti'jal" (seeking haste) is omitted; the implied meaning is: do not seek to hasten the punishment upon them. It has been said that the Prophet ﷺ became somewhat impatient with his people, and he wished that Allah would send the punishment upon those among his people who refused. So he was commanded to be patient and to refrain from seeking haste. Then he was informed that this punishment for them is near, and that it will certainly descend upon them, even if it is delayed. When that punishment descends upon them, they will consider the duration of their stay in the world to be short, until they reckon it as an hour of a day. The meaning is that when they witness the punishment, their long stay in the world and in the barzakh (intermediate state) will seem as if it were an hour of the day, or as if it had not been, because of the terror of what they see; or because whatever has passed becomes as though it had never been, even if it was long. The poet said:

It is as though a thing had never been once it has passed, and as though a thing had never ceased to be when it has come.

Know that the sentence is complete here. Then the Exalted said: (Balagh), meaning: this is a message. Its parallel is His saying: ﴿This is a message for mankind﴾ [Ibrahim: 52], meaning: what you have been admonished with contains sufficiency in admonition; or this is a conveyance (tabligh) from the messengers. So will anyone be destroyed except those who turn away from being admonished by it and from acting upon its requirement? And Allah knows best.

The author, may God Most High have mercy on him, said: The exegesis of this surah was completed on Wednesday, the twentieth of Dhu al-Hijjah, in the year six hundred and three. Praise be to God, Lord of the worlds, and prayers and peace upon our master Muhammad, his family, his companions, his wives, and those who follow them in goodness until the Day of Judgment.
